States/UTs. The Committee are shocked to know that even after more than three decades 
of enactment of PoA Act only 7 States/UTs have such police stations. The Committee are 
of the opinion that the setting up of Special Police Stations by the States/UTs is essential 
as victims first approach police station for protection at the time of atrocity and it is 
assumed these police stations would be able to address such situations more effectively.  
The Committee do not find any information regarding setting up of Special Courts also. 
The regular meetings with the State government over the years have also failed to yield 
the desired result. 
The Committee note that the Department has submitted a proposal before the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) to enhance the relief amounts and provide 
financial support to States for setting up Special Police Stations and Special Courts. The 
Committee hope that the Department should have incorporated the expected increase in 
funds for the year 2026-27 so that there is no shortage of funds to meet the expenditure 
likely to increase with the approval of the proposal. The Committee accordingly desire 
that the Department should take necessary steps to ensure that the proposal is approved 
at the earliest so that it is implemented from 2026-27 itself and the machinery is 
adequately strengthened.

opportunities through skill development and other income-
generating activities has not picked up been able to 
maintain the required momentum. The Committee therefore 
desire that the Department should make efforts to identify 
the problem areas and find the solutions so that the 

121  
scheme gains momentum in achieving the income-
generating initiative to effectively address the problem of 
poverty among SC communities. The Committee also 
desire that monitoring mechanism should be evolved in the 
Department of Social Justice and Empowerment so that the 
updated information is available with them for the projects 
sanctioned.  
 
 6.15 The Committee are pleased to find that the Scheme of 
Residential Education for Students in High School in 
Targeted Areas (SRESHTA) has been introduced to enable 
students from the SC community to receive better 
education. The Scheme runs under two modes. In mode 1 
fee is reimbursed to private residential schools affiliated to 
CBSE/State Boards for providing high quality residential 
education to meritorious SC students. The Committee had 
observed during the study visit to some residential schools 
selected under this mode that the students are finding 
difficult to adjust in the schools located in States other than 
their domicile State due to linguistic and cultural 
difference. The Committee accordingly recommended 
Department of Social Justice and Empowerment during the 
Examination of Demand for Grants for the year 2025-26 to 
examine the issue and suitably revise the Scheme to 
accommodate the students selected in the Schools 
selected under the Scheme in their domicile State. The 
Committee, however, found during the Examination of 
Demand for Grants for the year 2026-27 that 703 students 
have been given admission to the students in the academic 
year 2025-26 in the schools selected in the States in the 
State other than domicile State. Taking cognizance of non-
adherence to the recommendation of the Committee, the 
Committee express their displeasure and feel that should 
have at least examined the issue and reported back to the 

122  
Committee on the pros and cons of the recommendation 
instead of showing ignorance to the Committee on the 
subject. The Committee would like the Department to 
consider the issue and in the process they may take 
feedback from the students. The Committee expects 
positive response from the Department in this regard. 
 6.16 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment provides grants to the Non- 
Government Organisations/Voluntary Organisations for 
running and maintenance of the projects of 
Residential/Non-Residential Schools and Hostels for SC 
students. The Committee note that the number of Schools 
selected every year has gone down since 2023-24 as 142 
schools were selected in 2022-23, 137 in 2024-25 and 130 in 
2025-26. Similarly, the number of selected students has 
also declined from 16479 in 2022- 23 to 14281 in 2024-25. 
The Committee expect that the number of schools as well 
as the number of students should increase every year in 
order to achieve the objective of the scheme. The 
deficiencies due to which there has been a decline in the 
number of students and the schools need to be identified 
and suitable action taken so that the objective of the 
Scheme is achieved. The Committee desire that the 
scheme is duly popularized not only by the Central but by 
the State Governments as well to attract more students. 
The Committee expect that the Department of Social 
Justice and Empowerment will take suitable measures to 
overcome the deficiencies of the scheme. 
 
 7.38 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment has neither been able to exhaust the 
budgetary allocation nor achieve the targets fixed for 2023-
24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 under various components of PM-

123  
YASASVI. The Committee find that certain procedural 
issues such as pending Aadhaar seeding, bank account 
validation, utilization certificates (UCs), etc., are challenges 
before the Department in optimizing the utilization of 
resources and maximizing the targets laid down under the 
Scheme. The Committee note that despite various 
measures such as periodic review, third party evaluation, 
awareness of Scheme, etc. taken by the Department to 
address the challenges in implementing the schemes these 
challenges continue to recur year after year. The 
Committee have no doubt about the sincerity of the 
Department, but it would appreciate if suitable steps are 
taken so that the issues hampering the Scheme dies down 
once and for all and the Scheme is  smoothly implemented. 
The Committee also note that the income eligibility 
has been enhanced from ₹2.5 lakh to ₹4.5 lakh by the 
Department and has also introduced disability allowance of 
₹10,000 per annum from 2026-27. However, the Committee 
find that the Budgetary Estimate for 2025-26 has not 
increased for most of the sub-components of the Scheme 
for the year 2026-27. The Committee expect that the 
expenditure on the sub-components may multiply as the 
number of applicants may increase with the enhanced 
income eligibility and disability allowance.  The Committee 
would therefore, like the Department to timely assess the 
funds requirement for the year 2026-27 to meet the 
increased demand under each sub-component of the 
Scheme. The Committee believe that the Department will 
take all necessary measures to ensure that no applicant is 
deprived of the Scheme for want of funds. The Committee 
would like to be informed in this regard. 
 
 7.39 The Committee note that the target fixed for 2024-25 under 
Post Matric Scholarship Scheme was not achieved and the 

124  
same target was again fixed for 2025-26. The Committee are 
not sure about the status of achievement vis-a-vis the 
target fixed for 2025-26 as the Committee have been 
informed that the details of Beneficiaries are not available 
with them and will be available only when the proposal for 
2026-27 are received from the State/UT Government. The 
Committee are surprised to find that the target for 2026-27 
has been reduced to 34 lakhs in comparison to previous 
two years. The Committee feel that the approach of the 
Department appears to be that if you are not able to achieve 
the goal it is better to bring down the goal so that you don’t 
have to face the failure. The Committee are not satisfied 
with the way the Scheme is being implemented by the 
Department as they strongly feel that the Scheme can be 
considered successful only if the target fixed are achieved 
and the target for next year are enhanced.  The Committee 
are of the opinion that the target fixed should increase 
every year so that the revised estimates also increase 
consequently. 
 The Committee are happy to note that a proposal 
has been submitted for revision of the scheme to the 
Expenditure Finance Committee with regard to the income 
ceiling and scholarship rates. In view of the proposed 
revision, the Committee feel that the budgetary allocation 
made may not be sufficient as the number of beneficiaries 
is likely to increase significantly. The Committee hope that 
the Department will make all efforts to implement the 
proposals from 2026-27 and seek enhancement of the 
budget at the RE stage to meet the requirement of funds so 
that students do not suffer. The Committee expect that the 
proposal will be approved urgently so that the beneficiaries 
get the benefit in the year 2026-27 itself.  The Committee 
would like to be apprised of the effect of the changes 
proposed to EFC on the Scheme in their action taken reply. 

125  
 
 7.40 The Committee note that the Top Class Education in School 
Scheme for OBCs/EBCs/DNTs students started in 2022-23 
was proposed to be discontinued from 2026-27. The 
Committee are not able to understand the reasons for this 
proposal as large number of people benefitted from the 
Scheme in 2024-25 and 2025-26 and a similar trend is 
expected in 2025-26. Keeping the utility of the Scheme to 
the people, the Committee are happy to know that the 
scheme has now been approved for continuation in 2026-
27 and also believes that the scheme will continue beyond 
2026-27. Since the budgetary allocation of ₹ 20.00 crore for 
2026-27 is much lower in comparison to the budget of 
₹100.00 crore allocated for 2025-26 and the target of 40000 
fixed for 2026-27 in comparison to the target of 30000 fixed 
for 2025-26, the Committee expect that the Department of 
Social Justice and Empowerment will be able to meet the 
target laid down for 2026-27 with the limited budget so that 
the target section of the Society gets due benefit. The 
Committee would like to recommend for the continuation 
of the Scheme beyond 2026-27 in the interest of the society 
and would also like to be informed with respect to the 
utilization of budgetary allocation for 2026-27 in their action 
taken reply. 
 
 7.41 The Committee are happy to note that the Department of 
Social Justice and Empowerment has introduced a new 
scheme called SAMRAS for the construction of high-
quality hostels in Central Universities for students 
belonging to all categories including SCs, OBCs, EBCs, 
DNTs and even General category students. The Committee 
are not able to understand about the status of similar 
schemes such as Scheme of Hostels for SCs under PM-

126  
AJAY, construction of hostel for OBC boys and Girls under 
PM-YASASVI after the introduction of SAMRAS Scheme. 
The Committee may like to recommend that the Department 
should draw the modalities of the new Scheme SAMRAS as 
early as possible so that it can be implemented in the next 
financial year. The Committee would be happy if the other 
Hostel Schemes of the Department continues so that the 
students are not deprived of the Scheme as they have a 
dedicated budget for the targeted caste. 
11. 8.23 The Committee are happy to note that the Department of 
Social Justice and Empowerment has been allocated 
₹740.00 crore for the year 2026-27 under Atal Vayo 
Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY), over and above the allocations 
made for 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26. Unfortunately, the 
Department was not able to spend the Revised Estimate for 
2024-25 and has been able to spend only 60% of the 
allocation in 2025-26. The Committee hope that the 
Department will be able to spend the Budgetary Allocation 
for 2025-26 and would take necessary initiatives to rule out 
the reasons such as delays in approval, revision of scheme 
guidelines, etc., resulting in under-utilisation of funds. The 
Committee expect that the changes proposed to the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) will be approved at 
the earliest  so that the senior citizens can reap the benefits 
of the changes proposed from 2026-27 onwards and the 
budget allocated for 2026-27 is  also fully utilised.  
 
 8.24 The Committee have been made to understand that the 
Department proposes to associate State/UT governments 
for the smooth implementation of Schemes and also 
proposes to increase funding limit to Start ups under 
SAGE, increase in daily food nutrition, etc.  As per the 
proposal the Centre and State would be sharing 

127  
expenditure in the ratio of 60:40. The Committee are sure 
that the measures being proposed would enhance the 
performance of the Scheme in the interest of senior citizens 
but they are apprehensive for the 40% share of State 
government. The Committee do not want the Scheme to 
suffer for want of funds from State Governments. 
Therefore, they would like Department to take 
precautionary steps so that States timely contribute their 
share and the Schemes are implemented flawlessly.  The 
Committee would also like the Department to ensure that 
the proposal under submission is approved at the earliest 
so that the proposal is implemented from 2026-27 onwards. 
 
 
 
8.25 The Committee appreciate the efforts of the Department 
and the initiatives taken by it for the welfare of Senior 
Citizens over the years. In order to have better management 
the Department has proposed to associate State/UT 
Governments in the implementation of the Schemes.  The 
Committee also feel that the available machinery with the 
senior citizens Division of the Department is not sufficient 
to cater to the requirement of the senior citizens. The 
Department has also received suggestions from various 
quarters for a separate dedicated Department for the 
welfare of senior citizens. The Department should examine 
the infrastructure available in the Department to manage 
the affairs of Senior Citizens. As is already known that the 
population of Senior Citizens in the country is projected to 
increase from 8.4% to 14.9% of the total population by 2036, 
and a small Division in the Department cannot be expected 
to cater to the increasing population of senior citizens. The 
Committee would also like to draw the attention towards 
the creation of separate Department for Divyangjan in 2012 
by the Government. The separate Department was created 
to manage the affairs of comparatively less population of 

128  
Divyangjan in the country and is effectively catering to their 
needs. The Committee would also like to express that once 
the ‘Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior 
Citizens (Amendment) Bill, 2019 is enacted the 
responsibilities of the Division will multiply. In view of the 
large population of Senior Citizens which continues to 
increase every year, the Committee would like the 
Government to examine creation of a separate dedicated 
Department under the Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment as has been created for Divyangjan to 
ensure greater focus on policy matters relating to Senior 
Citizens and better coordination among stakeholders. 
 
 9.13 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice 
s Empowerment, in a joint initiative with the Ministry of 
Housing and Urban Affairs, has been implementing the 
‘NAMASTE’ scheme since 2023-24 for the safety and 
dignity of sanitation workers comprising Manual 
Scavengers, Sewer and Septic Tank Workers. The 
Department has also included waste pickers under the 
scheme since 2024-25. The Committee are happy to note 
that the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment 
has also proposed a new target group consisting of drain-
cleaners, workers at Sewage Treatment Plants and Faecal 
Sludge Treatment Plants during the next financial cycle, 
i.e., 2026-27 to 2030-31. The Committee finds that 89,248 
Sewer and Septic Tank Workers and 1,87,120 waste pickers 
have been validated, out of which 87,037 Sewer and Septic 
Tank Workers and 7,499 waste pickers have been provided 
PPE kits. The Committee appreciate the measures such as 
occupational safety training, safety devices, workshops, 
health insurance coverage, etc., taken by the Department 
since the initiation of the scheme in 2023-24. However, the 
Committee are of the opinion that profiling, distribution of 

129  
PPE kits and provision of occupational safety training to all 
sanitation workers will require greater effort, time and 
funds. The Department of Social Justice and Empowerment 
should therefore expedite the process and lay down a time 
frame to complete all necessary steps for the economic and 
social welfare of sanitation workers.  
The Committee also feel that the funds provided under the 
scheme need to be increased, as the Department has 
already spent 93% of the Revised Estimate for 2025-26, 
therefore, the allocation of ₹110.00 crore made for 2026-27 
may not be sufficient to complete the tasks undertaken by 
the Department as a large number of workers are still to be 
provided PPE kits and other benefits. Further, after the 
inclusion of the new target group from 2026-27 under the 
scheme, the Department may face a shortage of funds. The 
Committee would therefore like the Department to take 
sufficient steps so that basic facilities such as PPE kits, 
training and health insurance are provided to all workers at 
the earliest, and budget constraints should not become a 
hurdle, especially when several deaths of sewer and septic 
tank workers are still being reported. 
 
 
 10.9 The Committee note that the Department of Social Justice 
and Empowerment is the custodian of civic rights and is 
responsible for the prevention of atrocities against 
Scheduled Castes. Funds are allocated to the Department 
for strengthening of machinery for enforcement of 
protection of Civil Rights Act,1955 and Prevention of 
Atrocities Act ,1989. The Department has accordingly taken 
measures over the years for the functioning and 
strengthening of Protection Cells and Special Police 
Stations as envisaged under these Acts. The Committee 

130  
however find that though almost all States/UTs have set up 
Protection Cells but only 181 Special Police Stations have 
been established in only 7 States/UTs. The Committee are 
shocked to know that even after more than three decades 
of enactment of PoA Act only 7 States/UTs have such 
police stations. The Committee are of the opinion that the 
setting up of Special Police Stations by the States/UTs is 
essential as victims first approach police station for 
protection at the time of atrocity and it is assumed these 
police stations would be able to address such situations 
more effectively.  The Committee do not find any 
information regarding setting up of Special Courts also. 
The regular meetings with the State government over the 
years have also failed to yield the desired result. 
The Committee note that the Department has 
submitted a proposal before the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC) to enhance the relief amounts and 
provide financial support to States for setting up Special 
Police Stations and Special Courts. The Committee hope 
that the Department should have incorporated the 
expected increase in funds for the year 2026-27 so that 
there is no shortage of funds to meet the expenditure likely 
to increase with the approval of the proposal. The 
Committee accordingly desire that the Department should 
take necessary steps to ensure that the proposal is 
approved at the earliest so that it is implemented from 
2026-27 itself and the machinery is adequately 
strengthened.

INTRODUCTION 
 
  I, the Chairperson, Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment (2025-26) having been authorized by the Committee do 
present on their behalf this Eighteenth Report on 'Demands for Grants for 
the year 2026-27' pertaining to the Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment (Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities). 
2. The Committee considered the ‘Demands for Grants (2026-27)’ of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities which were laid on 
the Table of the House on 10 February, 2026. After obtaining the Budget 
Documents, Explanatory Notes, etc., the Committee took evidence of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities on 24 February, 
2026. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at the sitting held 
on 10.03.2026. 
3. The Committee wish to express their thanks to the Officers of the 
Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities for tendering oral 
evidence and placing before them the detailed written notes and post 
evidence information as desired by the Committee in connection with the 
examination of the ‘Demands for Grants (2026-27)’. 
4. For ease of reference observations/ recommendations/ comments of 
the Committee have been printed in bold in the body of the Report.    
 
 
 
 
 
 
New Delhi 
 10   March, 2026 
 19   Phalguna, 1947 (Saka) 
 
SHRI P.C MOHAN 
Chairperson 
Standing Committee on Social Justice 
and Empowerment 
 

1 
 
CHAPTER – I 
INTRODUCTORY 
The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) was carved out 
of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on 12 May, 2012 with the objective 
of giving focused attention to policy issues and providing a meaningful thrust to 
activities aimed at the welfare and empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (PwDs). 
Subsequently, on 8 December, 2014, the Department of Disability Affairs was renamed 
as the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. 
 
1.2 The Department acts as the nodal agency for matters relating to disability and 
persons with disabilities and is responsible for coordinating with various stakeholders 
including Central Ministries, State Governments, Union Territory Administrations and 
voluntary organizations working in the disability sector. The Department is primarily 
entrusted with the task of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities. The subjects, 
allocated to the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) as 
per Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules are:- 
i) The following subjects which fall within List I-Union List of the Seventh Schedule 
to the Constitution: 
ii) Indo-US, Indo-UK, Indo-German, Indo-Swiss and Indo-Swedish Agreements for 
Duty-free import of donated relief goods/supplies and matters connected with 
the distribution of such supplies. 
iii)  The following subjects which fall within List-III - Concurrent List of the Seventh 
Schedule to the Constitution (as regards Legislation only): 
iv)  "Social Security and Social Insurance, save to the extent, allotted to any other 
Department"  
v) For the Union territories, the following subjects which fall in List II -State List or 
List III Concurrent List of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, in so far as 
they exist in regard to such territories:  

2 
 
vi)  "Relief of the Disabled and the unemployable; Social Security and Social 
Insurance, save to the extent allotted to any other Department". 
vii)  To act as the nodal Department for matters pertaining to Disability and Persons 
with Disabilities.  
1.3 The Department also administers important legislations governing different 
aspects of disability for the welfare and empowerment of persons with disabilities. 
These include the following: 
i. The Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 
ii. The National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, 
Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 
iii. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 
1.4 To discharge its mandate effectively, the Department operates through a network 
of Statutory Bodies, National Institutes, and Public Sector Undertakings: 
Statutory Bodies 
 Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI): Established to regulate and oversee training 
programs for professionals in rehabilitation and special education, maintaining 
the Central Rehabilitation Register (CRR). 
 The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (CCPD): Set up under 
Section 74(1) of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, to safeguard 
the rights of PwDs and look into complaints regarding the deprivation of such 
rights. 
 The National Trust: An autonomous body discharging legal duties through Local 
Level Committees (LLC) and welfare duties through various schemes for persons 
with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental Retardation, and Multiple Disabilities.  
 
 

3 
 
National Institutes (NIs) 
The Department oversees several specialized National Institutes located across the 
country, namely: 
i. Ali Yavar Jung National Institute of Speech and Hearing Disabilities (Divyangjan) 
(AYNISHD), Mumbai 
ii. National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPID), Secunderabad 
iii. National Institute for the Empowerment of Persons with Visual Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPVD), Dehradun 
iv. National Institute of Mental Health Rehabilitation (NIMHR), Sehore, Madhya 
Pradesh 
v. Swami Vivekanand National Institute of Rehabilitation Training and Research 
(SVNIRTAR), Cuttack 
vi. National Institute for Locomotor Disabilities (Divyangjan) (NILD), Kolkata 
vii. Pt. Deendayal Upadhyaya National Institute for Persons with Physical Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (PDUNIPPD), New Delhi 
viii. National Institute for Empowerment of Persons with Multiple Disabilities 
(Divyangjan) (NIEPMD), Chennai 
ix. Atal Bihari Vajpayee Center for Disability Sports (CDS), Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh 
x. Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre (ISLRTC), New Delhi. 
 
1.5 In addition to its statutory and research frameworks, the Department exercises 
administrative control over the following Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), 
which are tasked with providing financial assistance and manufacturing high-quality 
rehabilitative aids: 
i. National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corporation (NDFDC) 
ii. Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of India (ALIMCO), Kanpur 
 

4 
 
1.6 Disability in India is today largely defined by the provisions laid down under the 
RPwD Act 2016 which has been brought into force from April 19, 2017.The Act identifies 
various specified disabilities which have been broadly classified into five categories as 
under:- 
Types of 
Disabilities 
Components 
Physical Disability: (i) Locomotor Disability including Leprosy cured person, 
Cerebral Palsy, Dwarfism, Muscular Dystrophy Acid attack 
victims 
(ii) Visual Impairment (only Blindness and Low Vision) 
(iii) Hearing Impairment (only Deaf and Hard of Hearing) 
 
 Speech and 
Language Disability 
 
Intellectual Disability Specific Learning Disability, Autism Spectrum Disorder 
Mental Behavior 
(Mental Illness) 
 
Disability caused 
due to: 
 
Chronic Neurological Conditions such as Parkinson's disease 
and Multiple Sclerosis. 
Blood Disorder namely Haemophilia,  
Thalassemia and Sickle Cell Disease. 
Multiple Disabilities  
 
1.7 The Committee sought to ascertain from the Department whether there exists an 
updated and reliable estimate of the population of persons with disabilities in the 
country, particularly in view of the fact that the currently available figures are based on 
the Census of 2011 which is estimated at 2.68 crores and that the scope of recognized 
disabilities has since been expanded under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 

5 
 
(RPwD) Act, 2016. The Department, during the course of evidence before the 
Committee, deposed as under: 
“When we talk about the exact population, the most common data to be harped 
upon is the 2011 census data. At that point in time, the 2011 census data it was 
2.68 cr. But now there are lot many caveats regarding these figures. Firstly, when 
the 2011 census was done, we had PWD Act 1995 in vogue. Our present RPWD 
Act came in vogue in 2016. In 2011, it was PWD Act, 1995 which was 
operational, and that Act mentioned only seven disabilities. Whereas right now, 
since 2016, we are legally recognizing 21 disabilities. That is the first point, there 
are 21 number of disabilities. ******** Now we have again requested the 
Registrar General of India to take into account 21 types of disabilities and to 
consult us whenever they feel like, so that the forthcoming census, whenever the 
results are out, we can rely upon those figures”.  
1.8 The Committee sought to know the mechanism adopted by the Department for 
preparing Budget Estimates in the absence of updated or latest data on the population 
of persons with disabilities. The Committee also desired to know whether the 
Government has any interim mechanism to estimate and track the changing 
demographics of persons with disabilities in the absence of updated census data. In 
reply, the Department submitted as under: 
"The Central Sector schemes being implemented by this Department namely 
SIPDA, DDRS, ADIP and Scholarship are demand driven and funds are disbursed 
based on the proposals received from States/UTs/Institutions/NGOs and 
individuals. The budget estimates are therefore prepared on the basis of previous 
years’ performance and expected demands rather than the population of persons 
with disabilities."  
 
1.9 The Committee note that the presently available estimate of persons 
with disabilities in the country is based on the Census of 2011, which 

6 
 
recorded the number at 2.68 crore. The Committee further note the

crore against the Revised Estimates of ₹1291.60 crore, which is only about 
78 per cent of the Revised Estimates. The Committee are of the view that 
such gaps between allocations and actual expenditure point to structural 
issues in planning, timely receipt of proposals, and coordination with 
implementing agencies. While the Department has indicated certain 
administrative constraints such as delay in submission of Utilization 
Certificates and late receipt of proposals from States/UTs, the Committee 
feel that these issues require a more systematic and proactive approach.   
 The Committee therefore recommend that the Department strengthen 
its expenditure management framework by instituting a more rigorous 
system of quarterly expenditure targets, real-time monitoring of fund 
utilisation, and advance identification of implementable proposals from 
States/UTs and implementing agencies. The Committee also urge the 
Department to establish strict timelines for submission of Utilization 
Certificates and proposals, and to introduce digital tracking mechanisms and 
periodic review meetings with States/UTs to ensure that procedural delays 
do not hinder timely release and utilisation of funds. The Committee are of 

16 
 
the firm view that such measures would help prevent concentration of 
expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year and ensure that the 
funds allocated translate into tangible and timely benefits for persons with 
disabilities. 
2.12 The Committee note that the major share of the Department’s scheme 
expenditure is concentrated in a few key demand-driven schemes such as 
ADIP, SIPDA, DDRS and the Scholarship Schemes, which together accounted 
for ₹741.80 crore in BE 2025–26 and have been allocated ₹1117.00 crore in 
BE 2026–27. The Committee observe that the effectiveness of these schemes 
depends significantly on timely submission of proposals, completion of 
documentation and submission of Utilization Certificates by States/UTs and 
implementing agencies. However, delays in these processes have been cited 
by the Department itself as major reasons for under-utilisation of funds in 
previous years The Committee therefore recommend that the Department 
put in place a structured mechanism for advance planning of proposals, 
periodic engagement with State Governments and implementing agencies, 
and a streamlined process for verification of documentation so that funds 
earmarked under these major schemes are released and utilised in a timely 
manner. The Committee further recommend that the Department may 
strengthen the monitoring system for tracking proposals, approvals and fund 
releases under each scheme, thereby ensuring greater transparency and 
efficiency in implementation. 
2.13 The Committee note that the Budget Estimates for the year 2026–27 
have been significantly enhanced to ₹1669.72 crore, reflecting an increase of 
about 30.96 per cent over the Budget Estimates of ₹1275.00 crore for the 
year 2025–26. While welcoming the enhanced allocation, the Committee 
emphasise that the increased outlay must lead to measurable improvements 
in service delivery and outreach to persons with disabilities. The Committee 
therefore recommend that the Department adopt a more outcome-oriented 

17 
 
approach in implementation of its schemes, with clearly defined physical 
targets, periodic evaluation of progress and stronger monitoring of 
implementation across States and Union Territories. The Committee also 
urge the Department to prioritise expansion of assistive device distribution, 
rehabilitation services, scholarships and skill development programmes, 
particularly in the North-Eastern Region and aspirational districts. The 
Committee are of the view that such targeted and outcome-focused 
utilisation of the enhanced allocation will ensure that the increased 
budgetary support translates into meaningful and tangible benefits for 
persons with disabilities across the country.

CHAPTER-III 
 
ASSISTANCE TO PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES FOR PURCHASE/FITTING  
OF AIDS/APPLIANCES (ADIP) 
 
 The Scheme of Assistance to Persons with Disabilities for Purchase/Fitting of Aids 
/Appliances (ADIP Scheme), launched in 1981 by the Government of India, aims to 
empower persons with disabilities (PwDs) by supplying scientifically manufactured, 
durable, modern, and cost effective aids and assistive devices that promote their 
physical, social and psychological rehabilitation, reduce the effects of disabilities, and 
enhance beneficiaries’ educational and economic potential. The Scheme was last revised 
w.e.f. 26.09.2024 and the major modifications undertaken are as under: 
a) “Since, ADIP is 100% central Sector Scheme, the requirement of State 
Government recommendations has been removed for receiving proposals. 
b) Data of assessment of beneficiaries and distribution of aids & assistive 
devices has been made mandatory through ARJUN Portal. Also beneficiaries 
can register themselves on the ARJUN Portal for requisite aids and appliance. 
ARJUN Portal is developed and maintained by ALIMCO, a CPSE under this 
Department ensures proper implementation and monitoring of the Scheme. 
c) The Department has taken a major step of opening Pradhan Mantri Divyasha 
Kendra (PMDK) of ALIMCO. These PMDKs are the walk-in centres where 
eligible beneficiary can directly avail required aids and appliances free of cost 
by visiting these centers.  
d) Eligibility of high-end Prosthesis has been reduced from 80% disability to 
40% disability. 
e) Under ADIP SSA eligibility for Motorized Tricycle has been relaxed 80% 
disability to 40% disability. 

19 
 
f) Benefits of ADIP SSA has also been extended to students studying through 
home Schooling and Special Schools. 
g) Age of Children criteria for availing aids and assistive devices every one year 
has been increased from 12 years to 18 years for customized items. 
h) Provision for self-certification of income by beneficiaries themselves has been 
introduced. 
i) In case of amputees without any disability certificate may also be provided 
with the benefit of Artificial Limbs only after the recommendation of P&O 
officials of ALIMCO/NIs/CRCs and enrolment for UDID Card. 
j) Inclusion of Motorized Tricycle with Li-Iron-Phosphate batteries in ADIP 
scheme with subsidy up to Rs 50,000.00 in line with recent advancement and 
towards green environment.  
k) Inclusion of Folding Joystick wheelchair in ADIP scheme with subsidy up to 
₹50,000/- 
l) Inclusion of Active Folding Wheelchair in ADIP scheme for high activity 
Divyangjan.”  
3.2 The Committee desired to know the thrust areas under the ADIP Scheme and the 
action plan proposed for the year 2026–27, particularly when the proposed 
modifications to the Scheme are awaiting approval of the Expenditure Finance 
Committee (EFC). In reply, the Department submitted as under: 
“Implementation of the ADIP Scheme shall continue as per the existing approved 
guidelines until the proposed modifications receive approval from the 
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) for next cycle. The thrust areas of the 
Scheme include strengthening outreach and service delivery through 
establishment of Pradhan Mantri Divyasha-Vayoshri Kendra (PMD-VK Centres) 
across districts in coordination with Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation of 
India (ALIMCO) to provide aids and assistive devices to walk-in Divyangjan, 
thereby enhancing last-mile delivery. The Scheme also focuses on organizing 
identification and distribution camps in remote regions, Aspirational Blocks, and 

20 
 
other unserved or underserved areas to ensure wider and equitable coverage. 
Further, emphasis is being placed on inclusion of modern, technologically 
advanced and high-end assistive devices to improve functionality and overall 
quality of life of beneficiaries. Transparency and accountability are being 
reinforced through beneficiary authentication and real-time monitoring via the 
ARJUN Portal.”  
3.3 The Committee further sought to know the reasons for revision of the Scheme in 
2022 and 2024 and the extent to which these revisions have been effective in serving 
the interests of Divyangjan. In reply, the Department submitted as under: 
“The 14th Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) cycle was completed in 2020. 
With the objective of expanding outreach, enhancing user-friendliness, and 
ensuring distribution of improved quality aids and assistive devices, the ADIP 
Scheme was subsequently revised in 2022 and again in 2024. 
The impact of these revisions has been significant. Since simplification of the 
Scheme w.e.f. 26.09.2024, a total of 3,92,638 beneficiaries have been covered. 
Out of these, 4,457 Divyangjan have been provided high-end prostheses. 
Additionally, advanced mobility devices such as motorized tricycles, motorized 
tricycles with Li-Ion batteries, joystick-operated wheelchairs (including non-
folding variants) have been provided to 40,081 Divyangjan under the ADIP 
Scheme. Out of these, 568 Motorized Tricycles has been distributed under ADIP-
SSA (Sarva Siksha Abhiyan). These measures have enhanced accessibility, 
expanded coverage of advanced assistive devices, and strengthened service 
delivery in the interest of Divyangjan.”  
3.4 The Department has implemented significant policy revisions in 2022 and 2024 
and the Budget Estimates for the Scheme have remained largely stagnant. 
Consequently, on being sought to provide a detailed clarification on the fiscal 
mechanisms employed by the Department to accommodate the resultant financial 

21 
 
implications within these existing budgetary constraints, the Department submitted as 
under: 
“The changes introduced in 2022 were necessitated by factors such as escalation 
in the cost of raw materials, recommendations of the Standing Committee 
regarding providing 100% subsidy for Motorized Tricycles, and the need to 
incorporate high-end devices to keep pace with evolving assistive technologies. 
These revisions, which had financial implications, were considered and 
accommodated during the 15th Finance Commission (EFC) cycle i.e. from 
01.04.2021 to 2025-26. 
However, the subsequent modifications carried out in 2024 were primarily 
procedural and aimed at simplifying the Scheme and improving ease of access 
and implementation. These changes did not entail any additional financial 
implications and were managed within the existing Budget Estimates.”

lakh against a target of 3.15 lakh in 2024–25, and 1.91 lakh beneficiaries 
have been covered so far in 2025–26 against a target of 2.05 lakh. The 
Committee note that the increasing provision of technologically advanced 
assistive devices has led to higher per-unit costs, which has moderated 
overall coverage. While appreciating the emphasis on improved quality of 
assistive devices, the Committee recommend that the Department maintain 
an appropriate balance between provision of advanced technologies and 
wider beneficiary coverage. The Committee further note that with 21 
categories of disabilities recognised under the RPwD Act, 2016, the demand 
for assistive technologies is likely to increase. Accordingly, as the 
Department enters the 16th Finance Commission cycle (2026–2031), the 
Committee recommend that the Department must present a realistic and 
adequately assessed fiscal requirement before the Ministry of Finance so that 
eligible Divyangjan are not deprived of assistive aids due to financial 
constraints. 
3.17 The Committee further recommend that the Department undertake 
periodic assessment of device-wise demand and cost structures and 
rationalise the mix of assistive devices provided under the Scheme so as to 
optimise utilisation of available resources and ensure wider outreach of 
essential assistive aids while facilitating access to advanced devices where 
required. The Department may also explore additional funding avenues, 
including leveraging the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds of 
CPSUs and private entities, specifically to bridge the funding gap for 

28 
 
expensive devices so that the primary budgetary outlay can maintain a wider 
net of beneficiaries. 
3.18 The Committee take note of the Department’s major initiative to 
establish Pradhan Mantri Divyasha Kendras (PMDKs) as permanent walk-in 
centers to facilitate direct access to aids and appliances. The Committee 
welcome this move to supplement the traditional camp-based model, and 
further recommend that the Department should also prioritize the expansion 
of PMDKs in Aspirational Blocks, remote regions and under-served areas to 
ensure that "walk-in" access is not a privilege limited to urban centers 
Furthermore, these Kendras should be equipped to provide minor repair and 
maintenance services for sophisticated devices, ensuring the long-term 
functionality of the equipment provided. The Committee suggest that the 
Department set a clear timeline for the conversion of all temporary 
distribution points into permanent, full-service PMDKs to ensure sustained 
last-mile delivery. 
3.19 The Committee note that the requirement of obtaining 
recommendations from the State Governments for proposals submitted by 
implementing agencies has been removed with a view to simplifying 
procedures and reducing delays in release of assistance under the Scheme. 
While the Committee appreciate the objective of expediting implementation, 
they are of the view that the removal of this layer of scrutiny may require 
stronger institutional safeguards to ensure transparency and accountability 
in the selection and functioning of implementing agencies. The Committee, 
therefore, recommend that the Department strengthen its due diligence, 
monitoring and audit mechanisms, including periodic review of implementing 
agencies and greater reliance on digital platforms such as the ARJUN portal, 
so that timely delivery of assistive devices is ensured without compromising 
oversight and accountability.

3.20  The Committee note that awareness activities are being undertaken 
under the Awareness Generation and Publicity (AGP) component as well as 
through initiatives such as Purple Fest and Divya Kala Melas. The Committee 
recommend that the Department further strengthen its outreach through 
greater use of digital platforms, social media and targeted publicity 
campaigns, so that information about schemes and services for Divyangjan 
reaches a wider section of potential beneficiaries across the country.

CHAPTER-IV 
DEENDAYAL DIVYANGJAN REHABILITATION SCHEME (DDRS) 
 
  The Deendayal Divyangjan Rehabilitation Scheme is a central sector scheme of 
the Department to provide grant-in-aid to non-governmental organizations (NGOs) for 
projects relating to rehabilitation of persons with disabilities aimed at enabling them to 
reach and maintain their optimal, physical, sensory, intellectual, psychiatric or socio-
functional levels.  
4.2  The Grant-in-aid is provided to Implementing agencies (IAs) which are registered 
with NGO-Darpan Portal of NITI Aayog and have obtained unique ID of NITI Aayog. 
The Grant-in-Aid (GIA) is provided through e-Anudaan portal of the Department. All 
financial assistance is provided to the Implementing agencies through Public Financial 
Management System (PFMS).  
There are eight model projects under the DDRS Scheme.  
i. Cross Disability Pre-Schools and Early Intervention with option for Home 
Based Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project  
ii. Special School for the Children with Hearing Disability with option for 
Home Based Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project  
iii. Special School for the children with Visual Disability (including Deaf 
blindness) with option for Home Based Rehabilitation and Community 
Based Rehabilitation Project and Low Vision Centre Project. 
iv. Special School for the children with other disabilities (ID/CP/ASD/MD/ 
Muscular Dystrophy, Deaf blindness etc.) with option for Home Based 
Rehabilitation and Community-Based Rehabilitation Project. 
v. Rehabilitation of Leprosy Cured Persons with option for Home-Based 
Rehabilitation & Community-Based Rehabilitation Project. 

31 
 
vi. Half Way Home for Psycho-Social Rehabilitation of Treated and Controlled 
individuals with Mental Illness with option for Home-Based Rehabilitation 
& Community-Based Rehabilitation Project vii. Preparatory / Remediation 
Centre for Children with Specific Learning Disabilities to continue Inclusive 
Education Project. 
vii. Cross-Disability Therapy and Counseling Centre Project. 
Activities/components admissible for grant under DDRS include:  
Honorarium to staff, Transportation of beneficiaries, Stipend for 
beneficiaries/hostel maintenance Cost of raw materials, and Contingencies to 
meet office expenses, electricity & water charges, rent, furniture, equipment etc.  
The eligibility conditions for Grants under DDRS are as under:  
Organizations registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 (XXI of 1860) 
or any relevant Act of the State/Union Territory; or A Trust registered under the 
Indian Trust Act, 1882 or any other similar Act for the time being in force; or, A 
Not-for-Profit company registered under Companies Act, 2013 or any relevant Act 
for the time being in force. 
Registration should have been in force for at least 2 years at the time of applying 
for grant under this scheme.  
a. Must be registered in the NITI Aayog Portal (NGO-Darpan) Portal and 
obtain Unique ID of NGO-Darpan before applying for Grant under the 
scheme.  
b. Must be registered either under erstwhile Persons with Disabilities Act, 
1995 or Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
 4.3  The scheme has been revised and is effective from 1st October 2024, with no 
changes to the cost norms. The key highlights of the revised scheme, in comparison to 
the previous version, are as follows:-  

32 
 
a. If the organization has not received the full and final GIA of the previous year 
due to pending proposal at the end of the Department and an advance 
proposal of the current year has been received, then the GIA up to 25 % of

b.  In case of projects being run by the institutions/Autonomous bodies of the

basic minimum wages or additional services/activities or additional 
equipments, so that PIAs can provide the rehabilitation services to PwDs 
smoothly. This will be over and above the funding norms of the GoI.  
4.4  District Disability Rehabilitation Centre (DDRC)  
The DDRC Scheme is a sub-component of the DDRS scheme. Main functions of DDRCs 
include Early Identification and Intervention, awareness generation, assessment of 
need/provision/fitment of assistive devices, therapeutic services e.g. Physiotherapy, 
Occupational Therapy, Speech Therapy, etc., referral and arrangement of surgical 
correction, assistance in providing scholarships, skill training, arrangement of loans for 
self-employment, survey & identification of persons with disabilities through camp 
approach, assisting in the issue of UDID Cards, and to act as outreach centres for the 
services provided by the National Institutes and for promoting barrier free environment. 
Revised scheme is effect from 01.04.2023.

  SIPDA is an umbrella scheme of the Department comprising of following 09 sub-
schemes: 
i. Creation of Barrier Free Environment for Persons with Disabilities  
ii. Divyang Samarth Yojana [National Action Plan (NAP) for Skill Training of Persons 
with Disabilities and Incentive to Private Employer].  
iii. Unique Disability ID (UDID) Project  
iv. Awareness Generation and Publicity (AGP) with In-service Training and 
Sensitization of key functionaries of Central & State Governments, Local Bodies 
and Other Provider.  
v. Financial support to Study and Research on priority areas of disability sector and 
to Research & Development of suitable product, aids & appliances for 
empowerment of Persons with Disabilities  
vi. Assistance to Spinal Injury Centers (State Spinal Injury Centre (SSIC) and Indian 
Spinal Injury Centre (ISIC))  
vii. Cross-Disability Early Intervention Centre  
viii. Financial Support for Development of Accessible Learning Materials 
ix. Central Project Management Unit (CPMU) cum Data Strategy Unit    
5.2   The objective of the Scheme is providing financial assistance for undertaking 
various activities outlined in the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD 
Act). The RPwD Act, 2016 endorses the rights of Persons with Disabilities for access to 
education, vocational training, employment, public transport, built-up environment, and 
information and communication ecosystems and upholds their independence and 
dignity.

Department could fully leverage the EFC-approved financial ceilings and avoid 
constraining viable accessibility and SIPDA projects due to initial 
under-provision at BE. 
Expenditure during the first three quarters remained below 50% primarily due 
to transitional bottlenecks arising from implementation of the CNA/TSA model 
from 2024–25 onwards, as several States/UTs could not timely onboard and 
draw down already-sanctioned funds, and a portion of funds had to be 
refunded/returned due to non-withdrawal within the stipulated timelines, with 
spill-over effects on utilisation patterns in 2025–26. In addition, utilisation 
was constrained by delayed and incomplete proposals from State 
Governments/UTs and implementing agencies, pendency of Utilization 
Certificates (UCs) required for release of further instalments, etc. Further, 
SIPDA sub-schemes are inherently demand-driven, expenditure is contingent 
on actual demand from States/UTs/implementing agencies and timely 
submission of complete proposals and requisite documentation; consequently, 
procedural rigidities at the State level, inter-agency coordination delays and 

46 
 
capacity constraints collectively contributed to lower drawl of funds during the 
first three quarters despite availability of allocation 
Corrective measures are being pursued through a combination of 
strengthened appraisal, closer monitoring and more realistic financial 
planning.” 
5.6  With regard to the measures taken/contemplated by the Department for 
achievement of targets fixed for 2026-27, the Department has submitted as under:- 
“In order to address the shortfalls in fund utilization and to facilitate full 
appropriate utilization of funds, the Department has taken several measures 
such as: 
a) A committee consisting of Joint Secretary (SIPDA), Director/Deputy 
Secretary (SIPDA), and two experts in the field of disability duly examines 
the proposals for release of Grant-in-Aid (GIA) under the Scheme. 
b). The Department conducts regular follow ups with the concerned 
stakeholders to expedite the release of GIA under the Umbrella Scheme 
SIPDA, which includes frequent communications by the Department for 
obtaining the requisite documents and/or proposals for consideration. The 
regular follow ups are made with States/UTs for submission of pending 
utilization certificates (UCs) and/or other related issues by writing letters, 
Video Conferencing (VCs) and telephonic correspondences so that any 
proposal with incomplete documents might not be kept on hold. 
c). To ensure optimal utilisation of, the Department is aligning releases 
with a realistic assessment of the State/UT’s absorptive capacity and its 
ability to utilise funds within the financial year, so as to minimize instances 
of unutilised balances being remitted back to the Consolidated Fund of 
India (CFI) under the current CNA/TSA model stipulations. 

47 
 
d) Revised proforma for the relevant sub components have been introduced 
for inviting the proposals from NIs/CRCs/NGOs  
e)  New Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) has been made for relevant 
sub schemes. 
f) In most cases, the proposals are invited through Online Portal only.”  
5.7  The Committee note that the budgetary allocation and expenditure 
under the Scheme for Implementation of the Rights of Persons with 
Disabilities Act, 2016 (SIPDA) have shown significant volatility during the 
last 3 financial years While the Budget Estimates of ₹150.00 crore in 2023–
24 were reduced sharply to ₹67.00 crore at the Revised Estimates stage, in 
2025–26 the allocation was enhanced from ₹115.10 crore to ₹200.00 crore, 
indicating considerable fluctuation in financial planning. The Committee 
further note that in 2024–25 the Actual Expenditure stood at ₹44.16 crore 
against the Revised Estimates of ₹111.00 crore, reflecting utilisation of less 
than 40 per cent of the available allocation. The Committee are of the view 
that such instability and under-utilisation under an umbrella scheme meant 
for implementing statutory obligations under the RPwD Act, 2016 may 
adversely affect the continuity of key interventions relating to accessibility, 
skill development and UDID implementation. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department adopt more realistic budgeting and 
stronger advance appraisal of proposals, along with closer monitoring of 
utilisation certificates and project readiness at the State/UT level, so that 
allocations under SIPDA are utilised in a timely and effective manner. 
5.8  The Committee observe that actual expenditure under SIPDA has 
frequently fallen short of the allocated funds, with the Department 
attributing these shortfalls to transitions in the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) 
and Treasury Single Account (TSA) models, as well as delays in the 

48 
 
submission of Utilization Certificates (UCs) by States/UTs. While appreciating 
the corrective measures taken by the Department, including revised 
proformas and digital processing of proposals, the Committee recommend 
that the Department strengthen its coordination with States/UTs and 
implementing agencies through regular reviews and advance identification of 
projects. This should also include providing dedicated technical support to 
States and implementing agencies to ensure their financial systems are fully 
integrated with the TSA/CNA framework. This would help ensure timely 
submission of proposals and more effective utilisation of funds for improving 
accessibility, rehabilitation services and overall empowerment of persons 
with disabilities.

CHAPTER-VI 
 
NATIONAL ACTION PLAN FOR SKILL TRAINING UNDER SIPDA 
 
The National Action Plan for Skill Development of Persons with Disabilities (NAP-
SDP) is a component under the Scheme for Implementation of Rights of Persons with 
Disabilities Act 2016 (SIPDA) and was launched in March 2015 with the objective to 
enhance skills of Persons with Disabilities, enable them to have gainful employment/ 
become self-employed and to make them self-reliant and independent members of 
society. Training under NAP-SDP is being provided through various Government and 
Non-Government Organizations. The common norms prescribed by the Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) for skill training are being followed. PwDs 
with at least 40% disability in the age group of 15-59 years are eligible to avail skill 
training programme. The scheme is being implemented through PM-DAKSH-DEPwD 
portal.  
6.2  Under NAP-SDP, the funds are released to the training partners as per the common 
norms prescribed by Ministry of Skill Development & Entrepreneurship. The 3rd 
instalment of grant-in-aid for the skill training programme (30% of cost) is linked with 
placement and is released on 70% verified employment (continuous employment of 3 
months-desk and verified placement as per standard norms), with at least 50% 
minimum wage employment of the certified trainees.

whereas actual were only 9333. Similarly, for 2024-25, target of 15,000 PwDs was set

6.6  The Committee observe with concern that the physical achievements 
under the National Action Plan for Skill Development of Persons with 
Disabilities (NAP-SDP) have remained significantly below the set targets over 
the last three years The performance data reveals a widening gap: against a 
target of 17,000 in 2023–24, the Department trained 9,333 beneficiaries; 
this fell sharply to 836 trainees against a target of 15,000 in 2024–25, and

Hybrid Treasury Single Account (TSA) model, the continued shortfall in

training modules remain aligned with current market demands. The

monitored quarterly to ensure that the transition to the new Yojana results 
in a measurable improvement in both the number of beneficiaries trained 
and their subsequent placement in sustainable employment.

CHAPTER-VII 
 
SCHOLARSHIPS FOR STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES 
  
The Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD) is 
implementing the Central Sector Umbrella Scheme of Scholarship for Students with 
Disabilities.  The main objectives of these scholarship schemes are to 
empower students with disabilities to study further in order to prepare themselves for 
earning their livelihood and  find a dignified place for themselves in the society, as they 
face several barriers-physical, financial, psychological in pursuing studies and living a 
dignified life. 
7.2  The scheme consists of the following six components :- 
a) Pre-matric (for classes IX and X). 
b)  Post-matric (for classes XI to postgraduate degree/diploma). 
c) Higher education (for undergraduate and postgraduate degree/diploma in 
notified institutions of excellence in education). 
d) National Fellowship (for M.Phil and Ph.D. in Indian universities). 
e) National Overseas Scholarship (for postgraduate degree/doctorate from foreign 
universities). 
f) Free coaching (for government recruitment examinations and entrance 
examinations to technical and professional courses).  
7.3  Regarding the eligibility criteria for scholarship it has been stated as under : 
a) The scholarships are open only to Indian nationals.  
b) All the components of scholarships are open to students with benchmark 
disability i.e. 40% or more disability as defined in ‘Rights of Persons with 
Disabilities Act, 2016  
 

55 
 
Further, the applicants should have/possess:       
a) Aadhaar based biometric authentication. 
b) UDID/UDID enrolment with valid certificate of disability issued by the 
competent authority 
c) Not more than two children with disabilities of the same parents will be 
entitled to receive benefits of the scheme. In case the second child is a twin, 
the scholarship under the schemes will be admissible to the twin. 
d) Scholarship for studying in any class will be available for only one year.  If a 
student has to repeat a class, she/he would not get scholarship for that class 
for a second (or a subsequent) year.   
e) A scholarship holder under this scheme will not avail any other 
scholarship/stipend. No scholarship will be paid to the students under this 
scheme from the date he/she accepts any other scholarship/stipend.

7.10  The Committee find that the financial allocation under the Scholarship 
Scheme for Students with Disabilities has remained largely stable during the 
period under review, with the Budget Estimates ranging between ₹142.68 
crore and ₹155.00 crore during 2023–24 to 2026–27. However, the 
Committee observe that the physical achievement under the Scheme has 
consistently fallen short of the prescribed targets. Against a target of 43,520 
beneficiaries, only 29,374 beneficiaries were covered in 2023–24 (about 67.5 
per cent) and 23,085 beneficiaries in 2024–25 (about 53 per cent). Similarly, 
17,378 beneficiaries have been covered so far in 2025–26, indicating a 
continuing gap between the intended outreach and actual coverage. The 
Committee note the Department’s explanation that stricter verification 

65 
 
through e-KYC authentication, UDID linkage and the National Scholarship 
Portal has led to elimination of duplicate or ineligible applications. While 
appreciating the steps taken to improve transparency in the system, the 
Committee recommend that the Department intensify awareness campaigns, 
coordination with States/UTs and monitoring of pendency at the State Nodal 
Officer level, so that a larger number of eligible students with disabilities are 
able to access the benefits of the Scheme. 
7.11  The Committee note the Department’s proposal to introduce a uniform 
lump-sum scholarship structure for certain components of the Scheme from 
the next EFC cycle (2026–27 onwards) with the objective of simplifying 
calculations and expediting disbursement. The Committee also note that 
delays in verification and processing at various stages, particularly due to 
pendency of applications and prolonged scrutiny at the level of State Nodal 
Officers, have adversely affected the timely release of scholarships in several 
cases. The Committee are of the view that scholarships constitute a critical 
support mechanism enabling students with disabilities to pursue education 
without financial hardship. The Committee therefore recommend that while 
finalising the revised framework, the Department ensure that the scholarship 
amounts remain adequate to meet actual educational expenses and that 
appropriate mechanisms are put in place to minimise processing delays at

9.9  The Committee note that the National Institutes and Composite Regional 
Centres (CRCs) play a crucial role in human resource development, research 
and rehabilitation services in the disability sector. However, the Committee 
observe that a significant gap exists between the sanctioned strength and 
the present staff strength in many of the Institutes and CRCs. For instance, 
institutions such as SVNIRTAR, Cuttack (115 against 197 sanctioned posts) 
and AYJNISHD, Mumbai (121 against 173 sanctioned posts) are functioning 
with substantial vacancies. Similarly, several CRCs are operating with limited 
manpower and in some cases posts remain entirely vacant. The Committee 
are of the view that such shortages may affect the quality of training, 
research and rehabilitation services being provided by these institutions. The 
Committee therefore recommend that the Department pursue the matter 
with the Ministry of Finance for early approval of creation and revival of 
posts and simultaneously take steps to expedite recruitment to existing 
vacancies, so that the National Institutes and CRCs are adequately staffed to 
effectively discharge their expanding mandate under the Rights of Persons 
with Disabilities Act, 2016. 
 9.10  The Committee appreciate that the National Institutes are undertaking 
several important research initiatives in the disability sector, including the 
development of tools such as the NIEPID Indian Test of Intelligence (NITI), 
assistive technologies and innovations in rehabilitation sciences. The 
Committee also note that financial support for research and development is 
being extended through the SIPDA component on priority areas of disability. 
The Committee are of the view that the National Institutes should 
increasingly function as centres of excellence in research, innovation and 
assistive technology development. The Committee therefore recommend that 
the Department encourage greater collaboration of the National Institutes 
with premier scientific institutions, universities and technology agencies, so 
that indigenous assistive technologies, rehabilitation tools and evidence-
based practices are developed and widely disseminated for the benefit of 
persons with disabilities.

CHAPTER-X 
NEW SCHEMES INTRODUCED IN THE YEAR 2026–27 
 
The Department has introduced two new schemes during the year 2026–27, namely 
Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana and Divyangjan Sahara Yojana, with allocations of ₹200 
crore and ₹100 crore respectively.  
Objectives of the Schemes 
The Department in their written have stated that Divyangjan Sahara Yojana is a newly 
introduced scheme during FY 2026-27 aimed at strengthening the assistive device 
ecosystem for Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan) through enhanced provisioning of 
high-quality assistive aids and appliances, including modern and advanced assistive 
technologies. The Scheme will be implemented through ALIMCO a CPSE under this 
Department. The proposal is under consultation stage with Stakeholders However, the 
objective proposed by ALIMCO is as under: 
(i) Scaling up ALIMCO Manufacturing and R&D Capacity: With the 
increased demand for high-end assistive devices under the scheme, 
scaling up ALIMCO’s manufacturing capacity is essential to ensure timely 
production and supply. 
(ii) Strengthening and Expansion of Pradhan Mantri Divyasha–Vayoshri 
Kendras (PMD-VKs): With an endeavour to enhance outreach and to 
provide assistive devices to Divyangjan and Senior Citizens nearer to their 
doorstep with minimum waiting time, PMD-VKs are being opened across 
the country. As on date, 100 PMD-VKs have already been established. 
(iii) Support for Establishment of Assistive Technology Marts (AT-Marts): 
ALIMCO is in the process of establishing Retail Assistive Technology Marts 
(AT-Marts) to provide high-end, good quality assistive devices to 
Divyangjan and Senior Citizens.

CHAPTER-XI 
 
MONITORING MECHANISM 
The Department implements a number of schemes involving substantial financial 
outlays for the welfare and empowerment of persons with disabilities. In this context, 
effective monitoring and oversight mechanisms assume importance to ensure that funds 
released under various schemes are properly utilized and that the intended objectives of 
the schemes are achieved. 
11.2  In this regard, the Committee sought to know the monitoring mechanism put in 
place by the Department to prevent misuse of funds and to ensure optimal utilization of 
financial resources under its various schemes. The Committee also sought to know how 
effective these mechanisms have been in actual practice. In reply, the Department 
submitted as under: 
 The monitoring mechanism in the Department to prevent misuse of funds and to 
ensure optimal utilization of financial resources to achieve the intended objectives of 
various schemes  
is given below: 
a. Monitoring of the Scheme is undertaken regularly at the level of the Secretary 
(DEPwD). 
b. The organizations have to furnish an audited utilization certificate in time in 
respect of the previous grant (s).   
c. Implementing agencies are required to maintain an updated official website and 
upload complete details of beneficiaries, including particulars of aids and assistive 
devices distributed, on their website as well as on the ARJUN Portal. 
d. Proposals of NGOs are being received and processed online on e-Anudaan Portal. 
e. Mandatory Registration of NGOs on NITI Aayog Portal (NGO Darpan). 

81 
 
f. ‘Arjun Portal facilitates near real-time Monitoring of beneficiary data and also 
prevent & check duplication of beneficiaries. The Implementing Agencies have to 
mandatorily upload the data of beneficiaries on ARJUN Portal. Further, duplicacy is 
also checked through UDID card which has been mandatory for beneficiary. 
g. Sample checking of beneficiaries against the utilisation of Grant-in-Aid released 
to Implementing Agencies by nearest NI/CRC/ALIMCO or by the Department of 
Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities if required. Sample Checking covers at 
least 2% of aids & assistive devices provided to the beneficiaries. 
i. Periodic field inspections and sample checks by the Central Monitoring Unit(CPMU) 
team are conducted to verify distribution of aids and appliances and beneficiary 
coverage. 
j. The regular follow ups are made with States/UTs for submission of pending 
utilization certificates (UCs) by writing letters, Video Conferencing (VCs) and 
telephonic correspondences so that any proposal with complete documents might 
not be kept on hold for want of pending UCs. Due to these efforts, the pending UCs 
have been reduced. 
k. Under Pre Matric, Post Matric & Top class Education, the Department monitors the 
times lines of verification of applications, application status and through the NSP 
portal on regular basis for proactive intervention if bottlenecks are identified. 
l. National Fellowship for PwDs in implemented through DEPwD and disbursement 
through Canara Bank on DBT Mode. NDFDC has been nominated as Implementing 
Agency and CNA for smooth implementation of NFPwD Scheme. Further, 
m. National Overseas Scholarship, the scheme is implemented by DEPwD and 
disbursement through MEA and the Department ensures that scholarship funds are 
disbursed in a timely manner and effectively utilized, enabling PwD students to 
pursue their education abroad without financial barriers or delays.

 11.3  Replying to the queries on the challenges faced in the execution and monitoring 
of the schemes implemented through State Governments/UT Administrations, Non-
Governmental Organizations and other agencies, and the measures being adopted to 
overcome these constraints the Department has furnished the following details: 
ADIP Scheme: Under the ADIP Scheme, certain operational challenges are 
experienced due to its implementation through multiple agencies such as 
NGOs/National Institutes/CRCs and ALIMCO. These include delays in 
submission of proposal for grants in aid, Utilization Certificates, difficulty in 
organizing distribution camps in remote areas/hilly areas, and ensuring 
timely and accurate uploading of beneficiary data due to high-speed 
internet facility. 
To address these issues, the Department has strengthened digital 
monitoring through UDID card, the ARJUN and e-Anudaan portals, 
mandated NGO Darpan registration, enforced submission of audited UCs 
before release of further grants, and undertaken periodic reviews and 
sample verifications through NIs/CRCs/ALIMCO. These measures have 
improved transparency, streamlined fund flow, and enhanced accountability 
in execution of the Scheme. 
SIPDA Scheme: Owing to the demand driven nature of the Creation of 
Barrier Free Environment (CBFE) component, fund disbursement is 
constrained by the actual demand from State Governments, the timely 
submission of appropriate proposals and documentation, and the receipt of 
Utilization Certificates from implementing agencies. This demand-driven 
nature presents a distinctive challenge in target-setting and budgetary 
projections, as allocations cannot be pre-determined independent of 
demonstrated state engagement and proposal quality. Estimates and 
targets for the CBFE/AIC component shall be recalibrated at the beginning 
of each financial year based on historical expenditure trends and 

83 
 
demonstrated state absorptive capacity recognizing the inherent constraints 
of demand-driven disbursement. The Department recognizes that rigid 
allocation and fixed target-setting methodologies have created persistent 
mismatches between budgetary projections and actual utilization; 
consequently, Revised Estimates shall be arrived based on the 
implementable commitments within the financial year, ensuring alignment 
between allocations and achievable outcomes given the demand-driven 
nature of the scheme. The Department commits to demonstrating sustained 
improvement in fund utilization through reduced proposal-to-sanction 
timelines, timely UC submissions, accelerated project completion rates, and 
enhanced state participation, with measurable progress being periodically 
reviewed to ensure accountability in advancing accessibility objectives 
across all government buildings in all states and UTs under the increasingly 
integrated and data-driven implementation framework. 
Scholarships: The Department is not facing any challenges/constraints in 
execution and monitoring of the Schemes. However, the scholarship scheme 
is a Central Sector Scheme and implemented pan India basis and is a 
demand-driven scheme. To cover all area across the country, the 
Department publishes advertisements in leading Newspapers across the 
country twice to increase awareness of these schemes amongst students 
and other stakeholders All other types of media and social media platforms 
are also used for spreading awareness. The Chief Secretaries/Principal 
Secretaries of the States are also addressed to spread awareness of the 
schemes through various mediums of communication in their respective 
States/UTs. Also, the department is actively organizing meetings with State 
Nodal Officers (SNOs) to ensure effective implementation of the schemes. 
 
 

84 
 
11.4 The Committee find that the Department has put in place several 
monitoring mechanisms such as ARJUN Portal, e-Anudaan, UDID integration, 
NGO-Darpan registration, field inspections and periodic review at the level of 
Secretary (DEPwD) to ensure transparency and proper utilisation of funds. 
However, the Committee also note that implementation of several schemes 
continue to face operational challenges such as delays in submission of 
proposals and utilisation certificates by implementing agencies, gaps in 
timely uploading of beneficiary data and logistical constraints in conducting 
camps and outreach activities in remote and hilly areas. The Committee are 
of the view that such procedural bottlenecks weaken the efficiency of 
otherwise well-designed monitoring systems. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department institutionalise a time-bound compliance 
framework for implementing agencies, strengthen digital integration of 
monitoring platforms such as ARJUN, UDID and e-Anudaan, and establish a 
structured follow-up mechanism with States/UTs and implementing agencies 
so that delays in documentation, reporting and fund utilisation are minimized 
and scheme benefits reach beneficiaries in a timely manner. 
11.5  The Committee note that several schemes of the Department, 
particularly ADIP and SIPDA, are implemented through a large network of 
States/UTs, NGOs, National Institutes, CRCs and other agencies, which poses 
inherent challenges in ensuring uniform standards of implementation and 
monitoring. The Committee further observe that issues such as delayed 
proposals, weak absorptive capacity at the State level, pending utilisation 
certificates and infrastructure or connectivity constraints in certain regions 
continue to affect the pace of scheme implementation. The Committee are of 
the view that addressing these structural constraints requires stronger 
institutional coordination and capacity building. The Committee therefore 
recommend that the Department develop a comprehensive monitoring and 
capacity-building framework for implementing agencies, including regular 

85 
 
performance reviews, targeted training for State and NGO partners, and a 
robust data-driven dashboard for real-time tracking of scheme 
implementation. Such measures would help improve accountability, 
strengthen implementation capacity across States/UTs and ensure that 
public funds allocated for the welfare of persons with disabilities are utilised 
efficiently and deliver measurable outcomes.
